title: The history of purses
titleCn: 钱包手提包的历史演变

paragraphs.text: The oldest bag preserved in the history is from the Tyrolean Iceman. This nickname was given to a well-preserved natural mummy. The man reportedly lived between 3400 and 3100 BC.

In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, bags were called purses, exclusively carried coins. These purses were essential as pockets in clothing were not developed just yet. In the fourteenth century and without the pockets in clothing, a purse was attached to the strings from the waist. From the sixteenth century onward, priests often wore the purses, a hook with chains to which small things could be attached, such as keys, knife cases, scissors, and sewing tools. Since purses were often crafted from precious metals, they were also considered as a symbol of status. The design and accessories evolved in the course of centuries, but it wasn't until the beginning of the twentieth century that handbag finally replaced it. Bags and purses came in a variety of designs for a number of purposes, such as bags with clasps, leather pouches. These were all worn attached to the belt. The introduction of pockets towards the end of the sixteenth century meant that men's bags slowly disappeared in the course of seventeenth century. From then on, bags belonged to almost exclusively to the women's domain. In the seventeenth and eighteenth century, women's clothing was so large that one or two bags or pockets could easily be hidden underneath the skirt. Such pockets were usually worn in pairs, one hanging from each hip, hence the name thigh pockets. Thigh pockets remained fashionable for most of nineteenth century. The dark times of the medieval age gave way to manufacturing a curious portraits on purses. Medieval purses were not only used as coin purse, they also were closely connected with marriage. As a result, they commonly showed love stories. Interestingly enough, this connection is deduced from connection between the handbag and the fertility. Bags altered to serve their uses to optimize their wearer's way of life. At least such was the case with sweetie bags, which are the bags that filled with sweet-smelling material. In a time when personal hygiene was poor, sweet bags were stuffed with sweet-smelling spices to get rid of bad smelly. For example, lavenders or perfumed balls of cotton. In the long run, sweet bags were also stored with clothes and linens used for aromatherapy. The bag continued to be highly functional and had many different nicknames and uses. Purses were often used as decorative package for gifts, such as money, perfume, or jewels. Notably, towards the end of century, purses became more sophisticated, evolving from simple drawstring design to more innovative shapes with dynamic materials. Seemingly, texture and manufacturing attributes were the only details left to be stylized. For instance, the 1930s saw the Art Deco style arrival. This particular style specifically highlighted the abstraction, just like any time period which experiences new industrial materials. The bag integrates them as well as within its design. In this particular case, plastic and zippers were introduced to the bag. Once the 1960s began, the bag experienced a self-expression as if being dynamic and versatile wasn't already be part of bag's characteristics. The bag experienced a brave awakening. Specifically, colorful patterns and flower power introduced energy into the fabric of the bag. The end of the 1960s saw the shoulder bag return, and with it came a lot of buckles, all of which indicated that women and their bags were ultimately fit and ready for the beginning age of feminism.

All in all, the 1980s saw an expansion in active consumption. The bag quickly changed to accommodate purchasing power, providing logos to indicate the priorities of the owner. For instance, sports bags such as Nike bags matched athletic shoes were most popular at this time. As a result, both bags and even the briefcase specifically featured a pocket which were exclusively created to hold this new invention.
